title: Emerging Technologies Classification and Adoption Strategies (Module 8 deck)
author: Andres Fortino (course deck, user-supplied)
type: course analytical framework
locator: Slides 26-35 classification; 38-47 adoption rules; 45 Rule #7 (know the required adoption style for your job); 54 Module 9 preview (Implementing Emerging Technologies: Proof of Concept, Task Technology Fit, Killer Uses, ECTM, FRS)
supports: Bleeding edge: extremely new, high risk from instability; leading edge: crossed the chasm. Rule #1 wait for the crossing before adopting; Rule #2 use pilot projects to test untested or underdeveloped technologies; Rule #7 know the adoption style your job requires. Module 9 (implementation) lists proof of concept and task-technology fit as implementation topics.
does_not_support: Readiness criteria for a specific organization; the Module 9 deck itself was not available to this agent.

title: The Diffusion of Emerging Technologies (Module 6 deck)
author: Andres Fortino (course deck, user-supplied)
type: course analytical framework
supports: Rogers' factors apply to staff as internal adopters: relative advantage, compatibility ('can it be easily assimilated'), complexity, trialability ('how easy is it to experiment'), observability. Roles: opinion leaders and change agents; change-agent functions end with 'stabilize adoption and prevent discontinuance' and 'shift the client from reliance on the change agent to self-reliance'.
does_not_support: Measured readiness of any organization.

title: Assignments 3-5 specialist outputs (Innovation and Disruption; Promethean; Diffusion)
author: Minghan Liu
type: upstream team-agent outputs
supports: A3: compare staff-only, simple retrieval and the proposed agent before any pilot. A4: long-term significance carries Low weight on present decisions (incremental-counterfactual test). A5: FAQ chatbots in admissions are past take-off; tool-using recruitment agents are at innovators/early adopters (denominator rule).
does_not_support: Independent evidence; prior AI-assisted student analyses used as inputs.

title: Assignment 6 Emerging Technology Adoption Agent v1.1 outputs
author: Minghan Liu
type: upstream team-agent output
supports: Agent-based applicant support is BLEEDING EDGE (Rule 1: no adopt; Rule 2: pilot). SPS: proof of concept now (staff-only vs Violet/simple retrieval vs agent on about 300 approved or synthetic inquiries), gated G1-G4 to a bounded experiment (at most 10% of web inquiries, 8 weeks, staff approve every message, no record writes, stop rule). G3 compliance sign-off; G4 approval capacity confirmed. Handoff: can admissions staff the human-approval and content-governance work?
does_not_support: Independent evidence; an AI-assisted student analysis used as the upstream input.

title: Task-Technology Fit and Individual Performance
author: Dale L. Goodhue and Ronald L. Thompson
type: peer-reviewed framework (Module 9 topic per C1 slide 54)
supports: For a technology to improve individual performance it 'must be utilized' and 'must be a good fit with the tasks it supports'; moderately supported by data from over 600 individuals in two companies.
does_not_support: Fit of LLM agents to admissions tasks specifically; the course's own Module 9 treatment.

title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
author: Frank F. Xu et al. (CMU and others)
type: independent agent benchmark (reused from A4 register)
supports: The most competitive agent completed 30% of simulated workplace tasks autonomously; more difficult long-horizon tasks remain beyond current systems.
does_not_support: Current frontier performance after the tested models; production reliability.

title: Building effective agents
author: Anthropic
type: vendor engineering guidance (reused from A4 register)
locator: What are agents; When to use agents
supports: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool use; agents trade latency and cost for performance and carry compounding-error risk; start with the simplest solution.
does_not_support: Independent evidence of agent superiority or reliability.

title: Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027
author: Gartner
type: analyst forecast and non-random poll (reused from A5 register)
supports: January 2025 poll of 3,412 webinar attendees: 19% significant agentic AI investment, 42% conservative, 31% wait-and-see; over 40% of agentic projects forecast to be cancelled by end-2027; only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic AI' vendors judged real ('agent washing'). Stated causes: 'escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls'; Gartner recommends 'only pursuing agentic AI in cases where it delivers clear value or ROI' (SD Times report, 2025-06-30, opened 2026-11-08).
does_not_support: Measured adoption; the poll is self-selected.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education (Ellucian 2026 AI report)
author: Ellucian
type: vendor survey (779 administrators, 300+ institutions, 93% U.S.) (reused from A5 register)
supports: Institutional AI use 66% (49% in 2024); 36% of Marketing, Admissions and Enrollment respondents use chatbots for FAQs; data security/privacy is the top institutional barrier (56%); 14% of executive respondents report a dedicated AI budget. No share for AI agents is reported.
does_not_support: Representativeness (vendor customers and contacts); agentic use.

title: Survey: Higher Ed AI Adoption Faces Financial, Policy Hurdles (EDUCAUSE 2025 AI Landscape Study)
author: GovTech reporting EDUCAUSE
type: secondary report of an association survey (reused from A5 register)
supports: 57% say AI is a strategic priority; 39% have AI acceptable-use policies; only 9% say privacy/security policies adequately address AI; only 2% fund AI with new sources; a 'widening digital divide' with larger institutions ahead.
does_not_support: Admissions-specific or agent-specific adoption; secondary report.

title: Meet the NYUAdmissionsBot
author: NYU Admissions
type: organization primary source (reused from A5 register)
supports: NYU Admissions offers a generative AI admissions bot on its admissions site and applicant portal, available 24/7; it hands off to a live agent or a contact form when it cannot answer.
does_not_support: SPS graduate admissions specifically; agentic actions; vendor; usage.

title: NYU SPS Graduate Admissions
author: NYU School of Professional Studies
type: organization primary source (reused from A5 register)
supports: Phone/email contact, weekday appointments, information sessions and 'For immediate assistance, try our chatbot, Violet.'
does_not_support: Violet's architecture, tool use, vendor or usage.

title: BC Tribunal Confirms Companies Remain Liable for Information Provided by AI Chatbot (Moffatt v. Air Canada)
author: American Bar Association, Business Law Today
type: secondary report of a tribunal decision (reused from A6 register)
supports: British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal held Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation after its website chatbot gave wrong bereavement-fare information. It rejected the argument that the chatbot was 'a separate legal entity'; the company 'still bore responsibility for all the information on its website, whether it came from a static page or a chatbot.' Damages were about CAD 650.
does_not_support: U.S. law or higher-education liability; a small-claims tribunal, not a court precedent. Used only to show that an organization owns what its conversational agent tells people.

title: Salesforce Introduces New Flexible Agentforce Pricing
author: Salesforce
type: vendor pricing announcement (reused from A6 register)
supports: Flex Credits: an agent action consumes 20 credits ($0.10 per action); packs of 100,000 credits cost $500; earlier conversational pricing was $2 per conversation; per-user licences were announced for later availability.
does_not_support: Total cost of ownership (integration, review, monitoring, correction) or current negotiated prices; one vendor only.

title: The AI Act implementation timeline: What changes under the AI Omnibus?
author: Future of Privacy Forum
type: secondary legal analysis (reused from A6 register)
supports: The AI Omnibus (published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026) moves Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 instead of 2 August 2026; Article 50 transparency obligations became generally applicable on 2 August 2026.
does_not_support: Whether a particular SPS use is in scope; any U.S. law. Legal determinations belong to compliance.

title: AI Act Service Desk: Education and vocational training (Annex III point 3)
author: European Commission AI Act Service Desk
type: official regulatory guidance page (reused from A6 register)
supports: High-risk education uses include AI systems intended to determine access or admission, or to assign persons to education institutions (3a), to evaluate learning outcomes (3b), to assess the appropriate level of education (3c), and to monitor prohibited student behaviour (3d).
does_not_support: Whether an applicant-support agent that excludes admission decisions is in scope; that depends on design and intended purpose and requires legal review.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1: Core (Govern and Manage functions)
author: NIST
type: public risk-management framework
supports: GOVERN 2.1: roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for managing AI risks 'are documented and are clear'. GOVERN 2.2: personnel 'receive AI risk management training'. GOVERN 2.3: 'Executive leadership ... takes responsibility for decisions about risks'. GOVERN 3.2: roles for 'human-AI configurations and oversight'. GOVERN 6.1: policies for risks from 'third-party entities'. MANAGE 2.4: mechanisms and assigned responsibilities 'to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems'. MANAGE 4.1: post-deployment monitoring incl. 'incident response, recovery, and change management'. MANAGE 4.3: incidents 'tracking, responding to, and recovering'.
does_not_support: That these practices predict success for a specific application; legal obligations. Voluntary framework.

title: A practical guide to building agents
author: OpenAI
date: 2025 (undated PDF; Prep Lab 2 required reading); accessed 2026-11-08
type: vendor practitioner guidance (course reading)
locator: 'When should you build an agent?' (p. 6); 'Plan for human intervention' (p. 31); conclusion (p. 32)
supports: Build agents for 'complex decision-making', 'difficult-to-maintain rules' and 'heavy reliance on unstructured data'; 'Otherwise, a deterministic solution may suffice.' Human oversight for actions that are 'sensitive, irreversible, or have high stakes'. 'Start small, validate with real users, and grow capabilities over time.'
does_not_support: Independent evidence of agent performance; vendor perspective.

title: The state of AI: How organizations are rewiring to capture value
author: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack)
type: global online survey (self-reported)
supports: Of 25 attributes tested, 'the redesign of workflows has the biggest effect on an organization's ability to see EBIT impact from its use of gen AI'; 21% of gen-AI users have fundamentally redesigned at least some workflows; tracking well-defined KPIs has the most bottom-line impact, yet under 20% track KPIs; CEO oversight correlates with higher self-reported impact.
does_not_support: Causation (self-reported correlations); higher education or admissions specifically.

title: 30% of Generative AI Projects Will Be Abandoned After Proof of Concept By End of 2025
author: Gartner, reported by MH&L
type: analyst forecast (secondary report)
supports: Gartner predicted 'at least 30% of generative AI (GenAI) projects will be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025', citing 'Poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value.'
does_not_support: Measured abandonment rates; agentic or admissions projects specifically. A forecast, used only to show where projects fail (after the proof of concept).

title: Higher Education Generative AI Readiness Assessment
author: EDUCAUSE (with support from Amazon Web Services); GovTech report 2024-04-25
date: PDF launched March 2024; web survey since; accessed 2026-11-08
type: sector readiness framework (association)
supports: A self-assessment of institutional readiness for strategic AI initiatives, 'separated into five sections: Strategy, Governance, Technology, Workforce, and Teaching and Learning'; intended to help leaders 'identify their strengths and weaknesses'.
does_not_support: Workflow capacity, budget and operating ownership for a specific application (not separate sections); scoring validity.

title: NYU IT Services, Apps, & Software: AI
author: New York University IT
type: organization primary source
supports: NYU IT lists Google Gemini, Google NotebookLM, Microsoft Copilot (in NYU Microsoft 365), Zoom AI Companion, Adobe generative features and an 'NYU Private GenAI Service' ('secure limited-access instances ... for NYU researchers who have a clear use case').
does_not_support: SPS admissions skills or use; which data may be used with which tool (not stated on the page); vendor agents.

title: How do I determine the security classification level of my data? (NYU Libraries FAQ); New Electronic Data and System Risk Classification Policy (NYU IT Security)
author: NYU Libraries; NYU IT
type: organization secondary pages describing an NYU policy
supports: NYU's Electronic Data and System Risk Classification Policy classifies data as low, medium or high risk; 'Always classify data with the highest applicable risk category'; the policy 'incorporates necessary General Data Protection Regulation' information and classifies assets into risk categories with required security precautions.
does_not_support: How applicant-inquiry data is classified; any AI- or vendor-agent-specific rule (the policy text itself was not opened).
